An automatic computing system is a device with which certain instructions can be given, and which will then carry out these instructions automatically. The device requires a central arithmetic part, a central control part, a memory that stores both instructions and numerical data, and input and output organs.

The IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic (IEEE 754) is a technical standard for floating-point computation which defines arithmetic formats, interchange formats, rounding rules, operations, and exception handling including binary32 and binary64.

UTF-8 encodes UCS characters as a varying number of octets, where the number of octets, and the value of each, depend on the integer value assigned to the character in ISO/IEC 10646. US-ASCII values do not appear otherwise in a UTF-8 encoded character stream.

Ownership is Rust's most unique feature and has deep implications for the rest of the language. It enables Rust to make memory safety guarantees without needing a garbage collector: each value in Rust has an owner, there can only be one owner at a time, and when the owner goes out of scope, the value will be dropped.

At any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references, and references must always be valid. Unsafe Rust unlocks five actions: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions, accessing mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits, and accessing union fields.

Safe Rust is a sound language: no matter what, Safe Rust cannot cause Undefined Behavior. Unsafe Rust is the exact same language with the same semantics, except that the programmer assumes responsibility for upholding the compiler's aliasing, alignment, initialization, and lifetime invariants.

Objects in C have storage duration (automatic, static, thread, or allocated), scope, linkage, and effective type. Dereferencing an invalid, null, or misaligned pointer, signed integer overflow, or violating strict aliasing rules results in undefined behavior.
